blocking.finding: The claim boundary misstates what the simulation base gives up. /clock reaches the backend through the same bridge publish callback and DDS path as the poses. The rule therefore cannot tell a stopped simulator from a stalled delivery path. L1's measured mechanism was exactly such a delivery stall: the bridge held a pose for 254.5 ms while the worker kept publishing. If the telemetry or delivery path stalls while physics and the command path keep running, the backend's /clock freezes along with the pose, and only the 2.0 s backstop trips. Three things let commands through during that time. In this profile the bridge does not zero commands on a STALLED feedback verdict. SCAN's controller keeps publishing commands computed from its last pose on a 10 ms wall timer. The Mac-side staleness rule zeroes only commands that stop arriving. Commands computed from a frozen pose can therefore reach running physics for up to 2.0 s of wall time, where v32 limited this to 0.25 s. The documents claim otherwise. PLAN.md:18 says a host stall stops simulated time. PLAN.md:94 says the only loss is a delay 'that leaves simulated time frozen. That is exactly the host stall v33 means to tolerate'. PHYSICAL_RUN_PLAN.md:57-58 says the run ends on odom_stale 'only if a pose stream truly stops, or the simulator stops for more than 2.0 s'. The recorded rationale for the backstop (PLAN.md:35-36) covers only a stopped simulator, not the converse. The case has been benign so far: simulated time advanced <= 0.08 s across all 128 recorded gaps over 0.25 s. The frozen statement is still wrong in principle.

non_blocking.finding: K4's M1 cannot fail on the recorded data. The single-threaded executor takes one pose per wait cycle from a depth-5 sensor-QoS queue, while the depth-1 /clock jumps to the newest value. M2 also ignores the burst of poses after a gap.
